title: Combined Oral Contraceptive Pill (COCP) Counselling
patient_instructions: You are Emily Nguyen, an 18-year-old university student who has come to the GP because you want to go on 'the pill'. You have a new boyfriend and want reliable contraception; a couple of friends are on it. Your periods are regular, moderate, not especially painful or heavy; last period two weeks ago. You are not currently pregnant and have only ever used condoms. You are generally well. If asked directly: you do NOT smoke, have no migraines, no blood clots in you or your family, no liver or heart problems, no breast or other cancer, blood pressure has never been high. You have NO significant medical history and take no regular medications (there is no epilepsy in this scenario). You had your Gardasil (HPV) vaccine at school. Your ideas: the pill is what everyone uses. Your concerns: you have heard it 'makes you gain weight' and you are a bit worried about clots because a friend mentioned it. Your expectation: to walk out with a prescription today. You are relaxed and cooperative. Ask at least one question, e.g. 'Will it make me put on weight?' or 'What do I do if I forget a pill?'. If the candidate offers you a choice of methods, say you are open to hearing about other options but had assumed you would just take a pill.
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice. Emily Nguyen, an 18-year-old woman, has requested 'the pill' for contraception. In the next 8 minutes: take a focused contraceptive history (including a screen for contraindications to oestrogen), briefly discuss the most effective contraceptive options including long-acting reversible contraception (LARC), and counsel her about the combined oral contraceptive pill (how it works, key risks, how to take it, missed-pill advice and safety-netting). Confirm her understanding. You do not need to perform an examination but should state what examination/observations you would do before prescribing.
examiner_instructions: Look for a structured history that actively screens the absolute contraindications to combined hormonal contraception (VTE personal/family history, migraine with aura, smoking >35yr, uncontrolled hypertension, breast cancer, active liver disease, <6 weeks postpartum). The candidate should proactively raise LARC (implant/IUD) as more effective than the COCP in typical use, rather than presenting the COCP as unconditionally 'first line'. Reward correct pre-prescription checks (blood pressure and BMI only; pelvic and breast examination are NOT required). Reward an accurate missed-pill rule (one missed active pill: take it and continue, no extra cover; two or more: condoms for 7 days and consider emergency contraception) and ACHES safety-netting. Prompt only if stuck: 'Is there anything you would examine or check before prescribing?' Mark communication on shared decision-making and checking understanding.

criteria: Explores reason for request, ICE and menstrual/sexual history
Systematically screens absolute oestrogen contraindications (VTE/family VTE, migraine with aura, smoking >35, uncontrolled hypertension, breast cancer, liver disease, postpartum)
States correct pre-prescription checks: blood pressure and BMI only; no routine pelvic or breast examination
Proactively discusses LARC (implant/IUD) as most effective and checks awareness rather than defaulting to COCP as 'more effective'
Confirms suitability for COCP given no contraindications
Correctly names oestrogen component as ethinyloestradiol (not oestradiol) using Australian spelling
Explains correct use: 21 active + 7 inactive, takes 7 days to work, condoms for first 7 days
Gives correct missed-pill rule (1 missed: take and continue; 2+ missed: condoms 7 days and consider EC)
Safety-nets ACHES warning symptoms and arranges 3-month BP/tolerability review; mentions emergency contraception options
Uses shared decision-making and lay language
Checks understanding (teach-back) and addresses weight/clot concerns

red_flags: Personal or family history of venous thromboembolism (DVT/PE) or known thrombophilia - absolute contraindication to combined hormonal contraception
Migraine with aura - absolute contraindication due to ischaemic stroke risk
Smoker aged over 35 years, uncontrolled hypertension (>=160/100), current/past breast cancer, active liver disease, or <6 weeks postpartum
New focal neurology, severe headache, chest pain, or unilateral leg swelling after starting (ACHES) - urgent review for VTE/stroke
australian_guidelines: RACGP / Therapeutic Guidelines: proactively offer LARC (implant/IUD >99% effective) as the most effective methods; COCP is a reasonable oral option (~91% typical-use effectiveness) but should not be framed as more effective than LARC

Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) contraception: standard COCPs contain ethinyloestradiol 20-35 microgram; only blood pressure and BMI are mandatory before starting - routine pelvic/bimanual and breast examination are not required

Emergency contraception: levonorgestrel 1.5 mg is licensed and most effective within 72 hours of unprotected sex; ulipristal acetate 30 mg up to 120 hours; the copper IUD (up to 5 days) is the most effective option - offer when presentation is beyond 72 hours
FSRH/UKMEC categories used in Australian practice for assessing contraindications to combined hormonal contraception
learning_objectives: Take a focused contraceptive history that reliably screens the absolute contraindications to combined hormonal contraception
Apply Australian shared decision-making by discussing LARC alongside the COCP rather than defaulting to the pill
Counsel accurately on COCP mechanism, correct use, current missed-pill rules and ACHES safety-netting
Use correct Australian terminology (ethinyloestradiol) and pre-prescription requirements (BP and BMI only)
key_points: LARC (implant/IUD) is more effective than the COCP in typical use; check awareness proactively
Standard COCPs contain ethinyloestradiol, not natural oestradiol; use Australian spelling (oestrogen)
Before prescribing you only need blood pressure and BMI - no routine pelvic or breast examination
Missed active pill: if one, take it and continue with no extra cover; if two or more, use condoms for 7 days and consider emergency contraception
Levonorgestrel EC works best within 72 hours; a copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception up to 5 days

citations.claim: LARC methods (implant/IUD) have higher typical-use effectiveness than oral contraceptives and awareness of LARC should be checked proactively, so the COCP should not be presented as the most effective 'first-line' method.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2473

citations.claim: Enzyme-inducing drugs reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives, informing counselling on interactions and alternative (LARC/progestogen) methods.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.3230

citations.claim: Contraception counselling, patient education and confirming patient understanding are assessed AMC communication competencies.
